A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
In the printed edition of the Diamond Sutra, before the scripture proper there is a verse called the 'Yunhe Fan' (the 'How Is It So' Hymn), which is extremely well written:
How may one gain long life, a body that ne'er decays?
And by what cause acquire a strength that never sways?
How through this sutra reach the farther shore's repose?
May the Buddha teach the subtle truth, and to all beings it disclose.

The first line, 'How may one gain long life, a body that ne'er decays,' asks how one can end birth and death and realize the dharmakāya. The second line, 'And by what cause acquire a strength that never sways,' asks: on the path of practice, when selfish desire and false views disturb the mind and the road forks in many directions, how can one gain great unshakable strength, undisturbed by the many confusions, and press straight ahead on the path of bodhi? The third line, 'How through this sutra reach the farther shore's repose,' asks how one can rely on this sutra (the Diamond Sutra) to cross the bitter sea of birth and death and reach the ultimate other shore of nirvāṇa. The fourth line, 'May the Buddha teach the subtle truth, and to all beings it disclose,' expresses the wish that the World-Honored One will broadly reveal and proclaim for all beings the rarest, most subtle, and most profound path to Buddhahood: how to attain the indestructible diamond body, how to gain great unshakable strength, and how to rely on this sutra to reach the ultimate other shore of nirvāṇa.
Question: What does 'Yunhe Fan' mean?
Answer: The three words 'Yunhe Fan' carry a double meaning.

First, in terms of its formal category, the 'Fan' in the Yunhe Fan means 'hymn' or 'Sanskrit chant' (fanbai), referring to the praise of the Buddha's virtues sung with exquisite sound. It is mainly used in lecturing on the sutras, in morning and evening recitation, and in repentance ceremonies at the place of practice. In all ceremonies — lecturing on sutras, receiving the precepts, chanting sutras, and so on — the Sanskrit chant is intoned (called 'making the fan') to still the clamor and gather in the mind.
[Bai] An abbreviation of 'beini' (bhāṇaka) — the intoning of sacred verses in the manner of Sanskrit chanting.

The 'Yunhe' in the Yunhe Fan takes the first two words of this verse, 'yun he' (how is it), as the name of this hymn. Similar hymns include, for example, the Tathāgata Hymn and the Dwelling-in-the-World Hymn:
The Tathāgata's wondrous form-body, none in the world can equal;
Incomparable and inconceivable, therefore now I pay homage.
The Tathāgata's form is endless, and so too is his wisdom;
All dharmas ever abide, therefore I take refuge in him.
Dwelling in the world like empty space, like a lotus that does not cling to water;
With a pure heart transcending all that, I bow and pay homage to the Unsurpassed One.
Second, in its deeper meaning, 'Yunhe Fan' means 'how to attain Buddhahood,' which is the core of this verse. The Abhidharmakośa says:
The Buddha corresponds with the unsurpassed virtue of Brahmā; therefore the World-Honored One alone deserves to be called Brahmā. According to the sutras, the Buddha is also called Brahmā.”
[Sutra] A scripture that both matches the capacities of living beings and accords with the truth — that is, a Buddhist scripture.
